performers: Sergei Rachmaninoff, piano; Philadelphia Orchestra; Leopold Stokowski, conductor
intro: Rachmaninoff recorded his Piano Concerto No. 2 with Leopold Stokowski and the Philadelphia Orchestra in 1929. In the first movement, Moderato, the opening bell chords lead into a running accompaniment for the strings, and this transfer contains only the first 78-rpm side.

sections.label: Intro · Piano chords over low F
sections.mNote: Piano chords repeat and grow before the orchestra’s melody

sections.label: A · First theme, strings over piano arpeggios
sections.mNote: The strings play the first theme in C minor.

sections.label: B · Piano takes the melody
sections.mNote: A quieter song within the opening movement.

cues.title: Opening chords, solo piano
cues.text: The piano begins alone. Each chord is followed by a low F, and the repeated strokes grow from pp towards f. Rachmaninoff writes a short ritardando before the hands move into the arpeggios beneath the first theme.
cues.evidence: Gutheil full score, Boosey & Hawkes reprint, p. 3: recurring low F, poco a poco crescendo, ritardando and a tempo. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/7/72/IMSLP528309-PMLP01953-Rachmaninoff_-_Piano_Concerto_No._2_(orch._score).pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: First theme, strings and clarinet
cues.text: In Stokowski’s orchestra the strings and clarinet play the C minor melody, and Rachmaninoff plays running arpeggios beneath it. Cellos and basses play pizzicato. The piano, which began the movement alone, now accompanies the orchestra’s long phrase.
cues.evidence: Full score, p. 4, rehearsal 1: first melody for clarinet and upper strings, piano arpeggios and pizzicato lower strings.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Recording session, Philadelphia, 10 April 1929
cues.text: Rachmaninoff and Stokowski made this recording at Philadelphia’s Academy of Music on 10 April 1929. They recorded the opening three times. Victor chose the third take, which was also issued in Britain on HMV D.B. 1333.
cues.evidence: Discography of American Historical Recordings, Victor matrix CVE-48963: session, venue, three takes and take 3 issued on Gramophone DB-1333. https://adp.library.ucsb.edu/index.php/matrix/refer/800022749

cues.title: First complete performance, Moscow, 1901
cues.text: At the première of the complete concerto in Moscow on 9 November 1901, Rachmaninoff played and Alexander Siloti conducted. Siloti was his cousin and former piano teacher. The last two movements had already been performed in Moscow at a charity concert the previous December.
cues.evidence: Marc Mandel’s BSO note documents the complete première, Siloti’s relationship to Rachmaninoff and the December 1900 charity performance. https://www.bso.org/works/piano-concerto-no-2-6

composer.epithet: Russian composer and pianist who earned his living at the piano in exile and whose music uses the sound of the bells of his childhood.
facts: Zverev and Siloti at the piano; Taneyev and Arensky in composition

quote.text: I feel like a ghost wandering in a world grown alien. I cannot cast out the old way of writing, and I cannot acquire the new.
quote.source: Rachmaninoff to Leonard Liebling, 1939; published in The Musical Courier, 5 April 1943

composer.background:
“My hearty thanks to the old man for not having forgotten about me!” Rachmaninoff wrote to the singer Mikhail Slonov on 26 December 1892. The old man was Tchaikovsky, who had praised his opera Aleko in a newspaper interview. Rachmaninoff was nineteen and had recently graduated from the Moscow Conservatory with its Great Gold Medal. Tchaikovsky helped get the opera into the Bolshoi, and in May 1893 he sat in the audience and applauded.

His childhood had been less settled. He was born into a landowning family and grew up at Oneg, near Novgorod, until his father’s financial failures forced a move to St Petersburg. He entered the Conservatory there in 1883. His parents separated, his sister Sofia died of diphtheria, and his schoolwork went badly. His grandmother took him to Orthodox services, where he heard the choirs and bells he remembered all his life. In 1885 his cousin Alexander Siloti recommended that he move to Moscow to study with the piano teacher Nikolai Zverev, who was known for his strictness.
